title: Aristotle’s Lyceum lay lost under Athens until building work uncovered it in 1996

cover.alt: Low stone foundations of Aristotle’s Lyceum in a sunken archaeological park in central Athens, with modern buildings and trees behind.

body: Around 335 BC, Aristotle returned to Athens and began teaching at the Lyceum, a sanctuary of Apollo Lyceus that had become a public exercise ground with a gymnasium, just outside the old city. His followers became known as the Peripatetics, by tradition because he walked as he taught. The school declined after him and fell with the city to the Roman general Sulla in 86 BC, and its exact spot was forgotten. In 1996, work to clear a site for a new museum of modern art uncovered the remains in the city centre, near Rigillis Street, and the ruins are now a public archaeological park.

slides.alt: A marble bust of Aristotle, bearded and with short hair, a Roman copy after a Greek original by Lysippos.
slides.caption: Aristotle taught at the Lyceum for about a dozen years, until he left Athens around 323 BC.

slides.heading: What was there before
slides.text: The Lyceum was not Aristotle’s private school building. It was a sanctuary of Apollo Lyceus that had become a public exercise area, with a gymnasium built later on, where Athenians trained and talked. Aristotle taught in that public place, and the name of the gymnasium became the name of his school.

slides.question: Why were Aristotle’s followers called Peripatetics?
slides.explanation: The name is traditionally linked to Aristotle’s habit of walking as he taught; the Greek verb peripatein means to walk about.

slides.prompt: What was about to be built when the Lyceum turned up?
slides.detail: In 1996, work to clear space for Athens’ new museum of modern art uncovered the remains. The site became an archaeological park instead.
